What separates real integration from an app store

Bolting together a Nest, a Sonos, three brands of Wi-Fi bulb, a Ring doorbell and a Yale lock is not a smart home. It is a set of independent apps sharing an SSID, each pushing telemetry to a different cloud, each with its own security posture. When any one vendor's cloud has an outage or an update, the corresponding feature stops working, usually silently, and the user is left tapping phones. The failure mode is the whole point of integration and it is the thing app-store setups do worst.

Real integration runs the automation on a local controller (a KNX line coupler, a Crestron 4-series processor, a Control4 EA-5, a Lutron HomeWorks QSX) with a wired backbone and a single defined set of scenes. Devices from different manufacturers are brought onto the local controller through certified drivers or protocol bridges. The system continues to work with the internet down; remote support is provided through a secured tunnel, not by exposing the controllers to the open cloud.

Frequently asked questions

KNX vs Crestron vs Control4: which do you recommend?

KNX is our default for lighting, HVAC and shading on residential projects because it is a wired open standard (ISO 14543-3) with a huge device ecosystem and no single-vendor cloud dependency. Crestron is often the right choice on a large, complex home or a bespoke commercial installation where the depth of integration and the customisation options justify the licensing and programming cost. Control4 sits in between for AV-heavy homes where the AV distribution and the automation should be from one vendor.

Wired or wireless?

Wired for anything permanent: lighting, blinds, HVAC, AV distribution, cameras. Wireless (Zigbee, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi) is used only where retrofit forbids the cable pull, or for peripheral devices (a remote sensor, a portable speaker). A wired backbone with wireless leaves the reliability of the whole system to the wire; a wireless-first system leaves it to the weather in the flat next door.

Can you retrofit an existing property?

Yes, though the wireless-to-wired ratio increases with the retrofit. On a whole-house refurbishment we install a full wired backbone. On a lighter retrofit we use KNX RF or wireless bridges where a chase is not feasible, accepting the reliability trade-off. On listed and mansion-block properties the routing is designed to minimise fabric intervention.

What is your cyber posture on remote support?

Remote support is provided through a secured tunnel initiated from the controller outbound; the controllers are not exposed to the open internet on inbound ports, and no automation credential leaves the local network. Building services (lighting, HVAC, shading, security) sit on an isolated VLAN separate from the user's laptops and personal devices, so a compromise on the user side cannot walk into the automation.

What warranty and spares provision applies?

12 months on installation and commissioning; manufacturer warranties on hardware (typically 2 to 5 years); a recommended small spares kit held on site (a keypad, a couple of switch actuators, a controller PSU); and an optional annual remote-support and firmware-management contract.

What training pack do you provide?

A written and PDF user guide with room-by-room scenes; a live walk-through with everyone who will operate the system (family, housekeeper, PA, security); a labelled diagram of the comms cabinet; and a set of quick-reference cards for common actions. Follow-up training visits are available under the support contract.
